product.title: Romanian 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Romanian: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Romanian builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Romanian is a Romance language, so hundreds of words already look familiar from English. Each unit targets one of the points that trip learners up most — from the definite article glued to the end of the noun, to three noun genders, to the subjunctive with să that replaces the infinitive. Includes a pronunciation guide, an A1 grammar summary, and a list of the core verbs with their participles.

blocks.text: Romanian is a surprise on the map of Europe. Surrounded by Slavic languages and Hungarian, it is in fact **a sister of Italian, Spanish, French, and Portuguese** — a direct descendant of the Latin that Roman soldiers brought to Dacia almost two thousand years ago. Its very name says so: *român* comes from *romanus*, "Roman".

For you, that means something very practical: **you already know a lot of Romanian words**. English absorbed thousands of Latin words through French and Latin itself, and the same words live on in Romanian: *familie, muzică, problemă, bilet, tren, doctor, farmacie, universitate, informație, telefon*. You are not starting from zero — you are starting with a few hundred words that only need a new sound.

The second gift is the spelling. Romanian is written **almost exactly the way it sounds**. The alphabet is Latin, plus five letters with marks — *ă, â, î, ș, ț* — and a handful of rules for *c* and *g*. After the pronunciation chapter ahead, you can read any word aloud, even one you have never seen. No silent letters French-style, no surprises English-style.

The third gift is more unexpected. Romanian puts its definite article **after the noun, glued on**: *tren* = train, *trenul* = the train; *casă* = house, *casa* = the house. It looks strange at first, but Scandinavian languages do the same thing, and after a week your eye stops noticing. Throughout this course, the word-for-word translation writes that article as *-the* (*trenul* → "train-the") so you get used to seeing it.

So where is the hard part? Romanian's difficulties are real, but they are gathered in just three places: **three noun genders** that decide the article, the plural, and the adjective endings; **verbs that change with the subject** — six forms for each tense; and **small pronouns** like *mă, te, îl, o, îmi, îți* that slip in front of the verb and love to merge with their neighbors (*m-am trezit, nu-mi place, l-am văzut*).

That is why none of the three is piled up at the start or pushed to the end. Gender comes in unit 3, the definite article in unit 4, plurals in unit 5. Verbs arrive group by group from unit 2 to unit 8. The small pronouns come one kind per unit: reflexive in unit 8, dative with *îmi place* in unit 10, accusative in unit 12 — each with a clear everyday job. The past tense only opens in unit 14, once the foundation is solid.
The explanations are short on purpose. What is long is not the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours broken into pieces. A language sticks through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.
Read aloud. In Romanian this is cheap: the spelling is honest, and the pronunciation column marks the stressed syllable in CAPITALS.

From the very first noun, note its **gender** together with the word — not *tren* but *tren (n)*; not *cafea* but *cafea (f)*. The article, plural, and adjectives cannot be guessed without it. This ten-second habit is what separates beginners who flow from beginners who stumble.

Don't wait for perfect pronunciation before you dare to speak. Romanians rarely meet foreigners who bother to learn their language; three words are enough to earn a big smile and, almost certainly, a cup of coffee.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Mult succes!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place, and the small pronouns arrive one kind per unit from unit 8 to unit 19.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — read the Romanian aloud first, without looking at the translation. Let your ear work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Word-for-word translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most, yet it is where you see how Romanian *thinks*. Example: *Cum te cheamă?* literally means "how you it-calls?", not "what's your name"; *Îmi place cafeaua* means "to-me pleases coffee-the".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt odd.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, with pronunciation and gender.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have really tried.

blocks.title: How to read the word-for-word translation
items: Hyphens join pieces that are **one word** in Romanian: *vorbesc* → "I-speak", *cafeaua* → "coffee-the", *fraților* → "brother-pl-the-gen".
**-the** = the definite article glued to the end. **a-m / a-f** = the indefinite article *un / o*. **m, f, n** = masculine, feminine, neuter.
**that** = the little word *să* that opens the subjunctive: *vreau să merg* → "I-want that I-go". Don't carry it into natural English — it is only a marker.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From unit 3 on, each unit asks you to review an earlier unit — two steps back, the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Romanian, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Romanian sentences from memory.
This is the part that turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit special to this course
items: Every time you meet a new noun, say its four forms in one go: one, the one, several, the several. *un tren → trenul → trenuri → trenurile*. *o casă → casa → case → casele*. Ten seconds per word, and articles and plurals stop being tables to memorize.
Every time you meet a new verb, say three forms: *eu*, *el*, and — from unit 14 — the participle. *lucrez → lucrează → am lucrat*. Those three are enough to derive almost everything else.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Romanian rewards this generously, because its spelling is honest — once you know the tables on the next page, you can read anything.

This section is short, and that is the good news. Romanian spelling is **almost completely honest**: a letter is read the same way in every word, with a handful of rules you can count on your fingers. Most letters sound much as you would expect — *b, d, f, l, m, n, p, s, t, v, z* need no study at all, and the vowels are always short and pure.
In the **Say it** column throughout the course, syllables are separated by hyphens and the stressed syllable is written in CAPITALS: *mulțumesc* → mool-tsoo-MEHSK.
Seven vowels

Five are the plain vowels of Spanish or Italian. The other two — *ă* and *â/î* — are the signature sounds of Romanian. Each vowel keeps its own spelling in the Say it column, so they never get mixed up.

Example
rows: **ah, ee, oh, oo** — always pure and short, as in *father, see, go* (no "w" glide), *food*
**î** — one sound, two letters. Lips spread as for *ee*, tongue pulled back as for *oo*

blocks.title: Two notes for English speakers
items: **You already have *ă*.** It is the relaxed "uh" sound English uses in *about, sofa, the*. The only difference: in Romanian it has its own letter, so *e* (eh) and *ă* (uh) are never confused. In this course's Say it column, *ă* is written **uh** and *e* is written **eh**.

**The *î/â* sound doesn't exist in English**, but it is easy to find: say a long *oo*, then — without moving your tongue — spread your lips as if smiling. That's it. It is close to the vowel in the second syllable of *roses* said lazily. **î** is written at the start and end of a word (*în, a coborî*), **â** in the middle (*pâine, când, român*). They sound exactly the same, and the Say it column keeps the letter **î**.

blocks.text: The c and g rule — the only one to memorize

The letters *c* and *g* have two sounds each, and the next letter decides which. The rule is exactly the same as in Italian: before **e** and **i** they turn soft; an inserted **h** makes them hard again.

head: Written
Sounds like
Example
rows: **c** + a, o, u, ă, â, consonant
**g** + a, o, u, ă, â, consonant

blocks.text: In the combinations *cea, cia, cio, ciu* and *gea, gia, gio, giu*, the *e* or *i* is just a softening sign and is barely heard: *ceai* sounds like **chai**, not "cheh-ai"; *ciocolată* sounds like **choh-koh-LAH-tuh**; *geam* (window) sounds like **jahm**.
Final i — the most often misread letter

**An unstressed -i at the end of a word, after a consonant, is not a syllable of its own**. It only *softens* the consonant before it — like a very short whispered *y*. In this course's Say it column, that sound is written with an **apostrophe**.

blocks.title: When a final i is fully pronounced
items: When it is **stressed**: infinitives like *a vorbi* (vohr-BEE), *a citi* (chee-TEE), *a locui* (loh-koo-EE).
When it follows a **consonant cluster + r or l**, because the word would be unpronounceable otherwise: *afli* (AH-flee), *negri* (NEH-gree), *metri* (MEH-tree).

When it is written **double**: *copii* (koh-PEEY) = children; *prietenii* = the friends. The first *i* is fully pronounced; in *prietenii*, the second is the definite article. You will meet this in unit 6.

blocks.text: Vowel pairs
Romanian loves gliding from one vowel to another inside a single syllable. These four pairs show up in almost every sentence:

head: Written
Sounds like
Example
rows: **wah** — one syllable, the *o* only a quick glide
**ai, ei, oi, ui, au, eu, iu, ou**
ai (*eye*), ey (*they*), oy (*boy*), ooy, ow (*how*), ehw, yoo, ohw

blocks.title: One small quirk: e that starts with y
items: A handful of very common words — the pronouns and forms of *a fi* — are written with *e-* at the front but **pronounced with y-**: *eu* (yehw) = I, *el* (yehl) = he, *ea* (yah) = she, *ei* (yey), *ele* (YEH-leh) = they, *ești* (yehsht'), *este* (YEHS-teh), *e* (yeh), *eram* (yeh-RAHM).
Other words starting with *e-* are read normally: *elev* (eh-LEHV) = pupil, *excursie* (ehks-KOOR-see-yeh). The y-list is closed — learn it once and you're done.

blocks.text: Stress

Romanian stress is **not fixed**, but it is predictable more often than not. Rough guide: words ending in a **vowel** are usually stressed on the **second-to-last** syllable (*CA-să, FRA-te, ma-ȘI-nă*); words ending in a **consonant** are usually stressed on the **last** syllable (*o-RAȘ, bi-LET, stu-DENT, res-tau-RANT*). Infinitives are always stressed at the end: *a lu-CRA, a ve-DEA, a vor-BI*.

There are exceptions, and no written mark shows them — which is why the Say it column always marks the stress. One reassuring fact: the definite article and plural endings **almost never move the stress**. *TREN → TRE-nul → TRE-nuri → TRE-nu-ri-le.* Once you know the stress of the basic form, every derived form is right too.
These pages are not for studying but for **coming back to** when you forget a form. Everything here was introduced one piece at a time in the units; it is collected here to be easy to find.
Articles — indefinite in front, definite glued on behind (units 3–6)

**Neuter = masculine in the singular, feminine in the plural.** *Un tren bun* (like m), but *două trenuri bune* (like f). **After a preposition, the definite article is dropped** unless the noun has a modifier: *în parc*, but *în parcul mare*. Exception: *cu* (*cu trenul*).
Genitive-dative — one form for "of" and "to" (units 13, 19)

blocks.text: Adjectives — after the noun, matching gender and number (units 9, 18)

**Comparison:** *mai mare decât* (bigger than) · *la fel de mare ca* (as big as) · *cel / cea mai mare, cei / cele mai mari* (the biggest). **Demonstratives:** *acest tren, această casă, acești studenți, aceste case* — or after a noun with the article: *trenul acesta, casa aceasta*.
Pronouns — four sets

These small pronouns stand **before the verb** (*îl văd, îmi place, mă trezesc*) and merge with *nu* and the past-tense auxiliary: *nu-mi place, m-am trezit, l-am văzut, mi-a plăcut*. Only *o* moves behind in the past: *am văzut-o*. A person as object is marked with *pe* and doubled by the pronoun: *Îl cunosc **pe** Andrei.*
Four irregular verbs that hold everything up
Present tense — four groups, six patterns (units 2, 7, 8)

Two things worth remembering from this table. First, in the *-a* group **el = ei** (*cântă, lucrează*); in the other groups **eu = ei** (*văd, merg, dorm, vorbesc*). Second, the *noi* and *voi* forms are always regular and stressed on the ending (except the *-e* group: *MER-gem, MER-geți*) — when in doubt, start from there.
The subjunctive with să (unit 11)

After *vreau, pot, trebuie, știu, îmi place, hai*, Romanian uses **să + a verb that agrees with the subject**, not the infinitive: *Vreau **să merg**. Poți **să vii**? Trebuie **să plecăm**.* The forms are the same as the present tense **except the third person**, which swaps the final vowel: *-ă → -e*, and *-e → -ă*.

head: Infinitive
el / ea (present)
el / ea / ei (subjunctive)
rows: să fie (full set: să fiu, să fii, să fie, să fim, să fiți, să fie)

blocks.text: Past and future (units 14–16, 20)

**Participle:** *-a → -at* (lucrat, mâncat), *-i → -it* (vorbit, dormit), *-ea → -ut* (văzut, avut), *-e → -ut* or *-s* (făcut, mers, scris, spus). **Imperfect** of *a fi* and *a avea*: *eram, erai, era, eram, erați, erau* · *aveam, aveai, avea, aveam, aveați, aveau*.
Numbers

head: Tens and up
rows: 100 o sută · 200 două sute · 1,000 o mie · 2,000 două mii

blocks.text: From 20 up, the number and its noun are linked with ***de***: *nouăsprezece lei*, but *douăzeci **de** lei, o sută **de** lei*. The numbers 1 and 2 (and those ending in 1 and 2) agree in gender: *doi frați, două surori, doisprezece ani, douăsprezece ore*.

The forty-six verbs that carry this whole course, with the three forms that let you derive almost any other: present *eu*, present *el/ea*, and the participle (used after *am, ai, a…* for the past tense).

blocks.text: If you reach this page after really working through all twenty units, you have a complete A1: you can introduce yourself, ask for directions, order food, shop at the market, buy a train ticket, say you feel sick, tell what happened yesterday, and make plans for tomorrow. More importantly, you are past the barrier that makes many people quit — noun gender, the article glued to the end, and the small pronouns that slip in front of the verb.
To move on to A2, these three things pay off fastest:

items: **The full imperfect.** In unit 20 you only got a taste of it through *eram, aveam, locuiam*. At A2 it becomes half the art of storytelling: the imperfect paints the background (*ploua, era târziu, mergeam spre casă*), the perfect compus drops in the event (*când am văzut-o*).

**Two small pronouns at once.** At A1 you use them one at a time. At A2 they come in pairs and merge: *mi-l dai* (you give it to me), *ți-o spun* (I tell it to you), *i le-am trimis* (I've sent them to him). It looks scary, but the order is fixed: dative first, accusative second.

**The conditional (*condiționalul*).** The *aș vrea* you have used since unit 4 is actually this form. Completing it — *aș, ai, ar, am, ați, ar* + infinitive: *aș putea, ar fi, ai veni?* — instantly makes you sound much more polite and flexible.

blocks.text: And one gift waiting for you at the end: Romanian is **a side door into the whole Romance family**. Anyone comfortable with *a avea, a face, a vedea, bun, mare, nou* will recognize *avere, fare, vedere, buono* in Italian and *haber, hacer, ver, bueno* in Spanish without opening a dictionary. Romanians themselves are famous for understanding Italian after a few weeks of watching Italian TV. One Romance language mastered is a big discount on the next four.

The language is spoken beyond Romania too: it is the official language of the **Republic of Moldova**, and large communities of speakers live in Italy, Spain, Germany, and the UK. Wherever you meet them, your first sentence has been ready since unit 1.
*Mult succes și la revedere!*
